transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. [Your Name]. Um, thank you for seeing me. I... well, I guess I'm here because I'm just really struggling right now. I just graduated with my bachelor's, which was supposed to be this huge, exciting thing, right? But honestly, it's just been a disaster. What finally made me come in—what really pushed me to make this appointment and actually show up, which is a miracle in itself—is that I keep forgetting basic adult things. And I mean really basic things. 

Like, paying bills. I will literally have the money in my account, I'll look at the bill, tell myself I'm going to pay it after I finish whatever I'm doing, and then it just completely vanishes from my brain until I get a late fee or a shut-off notice. And it's not just bills. It's returning emails for job interviews, which is so embarrassing. I had this one interview set up, and they emailed me to confirm the time, and I read it while I was walking to the kitchen, and I just... never replied. By the time I remembered three days later, they had already moved on. 

It's just constant. Showing up for appointments, following through on errands—like, I'll go to the store for three things and come back with none of them but a whole bunch of other stuff. It’s like my brain just drops things the second I look away. And it’s starting to cost me real opportunities, you know? Like that job interview. I can't keep living like this, feeling like I'm constantly dropping the ball on my own life. I just feel so overwhelmed all the time because I can't trust myself to remember anything important.
Can you tell me more about how you've been feeling emotionally lately? Have you noticed feeling down, sad, or hopeless most days?

Um, no, not really sad or hopeless. I mean, don't get me wrong, I get really upset sometimes. Like the other day, I was sitting in my car after realizing I forgot to mail this important package for my mom, which she asked me to do like a week ago, and I had the package literally sitting in the passenger seat staring at me the entire time. I just started crying out of pure frustration. But it's not like a deep, dark sadness, you know? 

It's not like I can't get out of bed because I'm so depressed or anything like that. I actually really want to do things. I want to get a job, I want to see my friends, I want to do my hobbies—like I just started getting into making my own clothes, which I bought all this expensive fabric for and then immediately lost the special fabric shears I bought, but that's a whole other story. But yeah, emotionally, it's more just... exasperation? I don't wake up feeling hopeless about the world or my life. I just feel incredibly annoyed with myself. 

I'm actually a pretty upbeat person usually, like my friends always say I'm the energetic one who's always ready to go do something or go out. So it's not a sad feeling at all, it's just this constant, overwhelming cycle of "why did I do that again?" and feeling like I'm running on a treadmill that's going way too fast and I keep tripping over my own feet. So, no, not really down or hopeless most days. Just... constantly frustrated by my own brain, if that makes sense?

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms primarily revolve around difficulties with attention, forgetfulness, and disorganization, which have persisted into adulthood and are significantly impacting their daily functioning. There is no strong evidence of a mood disorder (e.g., no persistent sadness, hopelessness, or loss of interest), which rules out recurrent depressive disorder codes (F33.0, F33.1, F33.2). The presentation is not consistent with adjustment disorders (F43.20, F43.21, F43.22) as the difficulties appear to be more enduring and not specifically tied to a stressor. Given the history and presentation, F90.0 (Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive type) is the most likely candidate at this point. No further questioning is needed as the clinical picture is clear and consistent with ADHD.
